verses.text: Some time later, the king's cupbearer and baker offended their master, the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker,
and imprisoned them in the house of the captain of the guard, the same prison where Joseph was confined.
The captain of the guard assigned them to Joseph, and he became their personal attendant. After they had been in custody for some time,
both of these men—the Egyptian king's cupbearer and baker, who were being held in the prison—had a dream on the same night, and each dream had its own meaning.
When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were distraught.
So he asked the officials of Pharaoh who were in custody with him in his master's house, "Why are your faces so downcast today?"
"We both had dreams," they replied, "but there is no one to interpret them." Then Joseph said to them, "Don't interpretations belong to God? Tell me your dreams."
So the chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream: "In my dream there was a vine before me,
and on the vine were three branches. As it budded, its blossoms opened and its clusters ripened into grapes.
Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes, squeezed them into his cup, and placed the cup in his hand."
Joseph replied, "This is the interpretation: The three branches are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore your position. You will put Pharaoh's cup in his hand, just as you did when you were his cupbearer.
But when it goes well for you, please remember me and show me kindness by mentioning me to Pharaoh, that he might bring me out of this prison.
For I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have done nothing for which they should have put me in this dungeon."
When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, "I too had a dream: There were three baskets of white bread on my head.
In the top basket were all sorts of baked goods for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head."
Joseph replied, "This is the interpretation: The three baskets are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree. Then the birds will eat the flesh of your body."
On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he held a feast for all his officials, and in their presence he lifted up the heads of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
Pharaoh restored the chief cupbearer to his position, so that he once again placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand.
But Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had described to them in his interpretation.
The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 37 to 50)
context.audience: Israel, the twelve tribes, learning how their fathers came down to Egypt and how God turned evil to good
context.setting: Pharaoh’s chief cupbearer and chief baker offend him and are put in the prison where Joseph is, and Joseph is assigned to look after them (vv.1-4). Both dream on the same night, and Joseph sees their downcast faces (vv.5-7). “There is no one to interpret them,” they say, and Joseph answers, “Don’t interpretations belong to God? Tell me your dreams” (v.8). The cupbearer dreams of a vine with three branches whose grapes he squeezes into Pharaoh’s cup; in three days, Joseph says, “Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore your position” (vv.9-13). Joseph asks, “please remember me,” for he was “kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews” and has done nothing to deserve the dungeon (vv.14-15). The baker dreams of three baskets on his head, with birds eating Pharaoh’s baked goods; in three days, Joseph says, “Pharaoh will lift off your head” (vv.16-19). On Pharaoh’s birthday it happens just as Joseph said (vv.20-22). “The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him” (v.23).
context.custom: The cupbearer was a close and trusted servant who tasted and served the king’s wine; Nehemiah held the same post in Persia (Nehemiah 1:11). Egyptians took dreams seriously, and a papyrus dream book of about 1275 BC (Papyrus Chester Beatty III) lists dreams with their good or bad meanings. Royal feasts and pardons on a king’s birthday or accession are known in the ancient world. Joseph plays on one phrase: Pharaoh will “lift up” the cupbearer’s head (restore him) and “lift off” the baker’s (kill him).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 41: two years later Pharaoh dreams, and the cupbearer finally remembers Joseph.
context.timelineBible: Joseph gives God the credit before he gives the interpretation (v.8), as Daniel later does before Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2:27-28). The forgotten prisoner waits two more years (41:1). Psalm 105 remembers the wait: “until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right” (Psalm 105:19). Jesus, too, was crucified between two criminals, one of whom asked, “remember me” (Luke 23:42).

translation.meaning: Interpretation, the meaning of a dream. Used only in the Joseph story (40:5-22; 41:11).
To lift up, carry. To lift up someone’s head meant to honor or restore him; Joseph turns it into “lift off your head” for the baker (v.19).
To remember. The cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but God had not forgotten him (8:1; 30:22).

gospelParallels.note: Jesus remember me when You come into Your kingdom.
Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them.
God has revealed it to us by His Spirit.

otBackground.note: There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.
I was cupbearer to the king.

overview.summary: In prison Joseph interprets the dreams of Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker; the cupbearer is restored and the baker hanged, but the cupbearer forgets Joseph.
overview.settingLine: The prison of the captain of the guard in Egypt.

history.t: Cupbearers and bakers served in Pharaoh’s household.
Royal celebrations brought pardons and punishments.

customs.t: Egyptians kept books for interpreting dreams.
Egyptians were clean-shaven; Joseph shaves before meeting Pharaoh in chapter 41.

archaeology.t: Papyrus Chester Beatty III lists dreams and their meanings.
Tomb models show Egyptian bakers and brewers at work.

overview.discussion: Joseph asked to be remembered and was forgotten for two more years (vv.14, 23). How do I keep doing faithful work when the people I helped forget me?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters. Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition
